title: Old Testament prayer (CCC 2568–2589)
hookLine: Abraham listens, Moses intercedes, David praises, Elijah waits

lines: AN OLD MAN: HERE I AM.
cards: Four people, four different places. An old man hearing his name called, and answering: here I am. A leader on a mountain, arguing with God for people who have just let him down.
A king with a harp, singing. A prophet in a cave, worn out, waiting for a voice that isn't in the wind or the fire. In the Catechism, these four are among the teachers of prayer before Christ.

teach.b: Abraham first; you watched him bargain for Sodom back in year two. The Catechism says his heart was in tune with God's will, and his prayer showed first in deeds: he went, as the Lord told him.
When God calls, Abraham answers, in the Douay-Rheims, "Here I am." Listening as prayer. Readiness.
And he dared to plead for Sodom: even the listener speaks up.
Moses next. After the people made the golden calf, he stands between them and God and pleads for them.
The Catechism calls this intercession, and notes that Moses doesn't pray for himself, but for the very people who made his life hard.

Exodus says the Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to a friend; intercession grows out of friendship. Then David, the king after God's own heart, a shepherd who prays for his people and in their name.
His prayer is praise and repentance, and tradition ties psalms to his name.
Praise, in his hands, is music. Last, Elijah. On Mount Carmel he prays and fire comes down.
Later he flees into the desert, exhausted, and on the mountain of God he waits. The Lord is not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire.

Then comes what the Douay-Rheims calls "a whistling of a gentle air," and there Elijah meets the Lord. Waiting is prayer too. Listen, intercede, praise, wait: lessons learned slowly, a long school before the Gospels.

how: The Church prays the psalms each day in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Old Testament readings are heard at Mass; the Catechism presents Abraham, Moses, David and Elijah as teachers of prayer.

games.q: you're Elijah, exhausted, on the mountain of God. a great wind, an earthquake, a fire. where is the Lord?
o: in a gentle air after them.
games.why: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in what the Douay-Rheims calls a whistling of a gentle air.

practice: Choose one of the four and take that posture: Abraham, simply ready, saying here I am if you pray; Moses, asking good for someone who has let you down; David, naming one thing that deserves praise; Elijah, doing nothing at all and waiting for the quiet underneath the noise.
Stay with the one you chose, whether you pray it or simply try it on.

wordCard.voice: Old Testament prayer. In Catholic teaching, the long school of prayer before Christ: Abraham's readiness, Moses' pleading, David's praise, Elijah's waiting. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: here I am — Abraham's answer when God calls him.

carryVoice: Your line: the long school. Readiness, pleading, praise and waiting all count as prayer. That's today, done.
